newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani rupee's strength seen short-lived.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani rupee's strength seen short-lived.

text.p: The Pakistani rupee has risen six percent against the dollar in kerb trade in the past four months but the gains may prove short-lived given an ailing economy and a strong dollar abroad, analysts said on Monday.
A foreign banker, who asked not to be named, said the rupee's show of muscle was a temporary phenomenon.

"With only $598 million in cash reserves and an estimated $350 million in debt repayments plus maturity of about $400 million in swap dollar funds falling due in February and March you cannot expect the rupee to maintain its present levels against the dollar," the banker said.
He said rising inflation and a worsening balance of payments would force Pakistan to devalue the rupee again sooner or later.
The rupee has gained 0.40 rupees to 40.90 against the dollar in kerb trade in the past week on hopes that pro-business prime minister-elect Nawaz Sharif will revive the economy.
President Farooq Leghari was due to swear in Sharif as prime minister later on Monday after he won a 177-16 confidence vote in the newly-elected National Assembly (lower house).

The rupee opened 0.02 up at 40.88 on Monday from Sunday's 40.90 close, compared with 43.50 on October 22, when the State (central) Bank of Pakistan devalued the rupee to 40.1200/40.3206 to the dollar from 36.9700/37.1549 fixed on September 10.

In the inter-bank forex market, dealers said the premium on six-month forward dollars had eased after staying at 10 percent for the past few days. On Sunday, offers were at 42.35 rupees as dollar demand from importers withered.
Most analysts said the rupee's recent strength was driven more by emotion than any deep-rooted economic change.
"It seems sentiment is ruling fundamentals at the moment," dealer Owais Kalia of Khanani & Kalia International said.
He said the rupee could fall back to around 41.60 as soon as the market recalled the reality of Pakistan's economic plight.
Kalia said most kerb players had used dollars to speculate on frequent rupee depreciations by the central bank. The rupee lost 17.14 percent of its dollar value in calendar 1996.
The official rate has been unchanged since the 7.86 percent devaluation on October 22 and for the past few weeks investors have been selling dollars to divert funds to the stock market.
The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index surged 4.99 percent to 1,721.07 points on Sunday and had added a further 14.36 points, or 0.83 percent, by noon on Monday.
Imran Iqbal, treasury analyst at BMA Capital Management, said many traders had switched from dollars to stocks.
"There is no change in fundamentals as economic problems remain unresolved, but there is a noticeable change in investors' perception," Iqbal said.
The consumer price index rose 2.17 percent in January over December, a year-on-year increase of 13.4 percent, up from 11.41 percent in December and 8.93 percent in January 1996.
The trade gap rose to a provisional $2.126 billion in the first seven months of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from $2.097 billion in the year-ago period.
Foreign exchange reserves, excluding gold, plummeted to $598 million on February 6 from $680 million on January 30.
"We see further erosion of the rupee by at least 1.50 to 2.0 percent by June," the foreign banker said.
Recent dollar gains in international markets could give the new government an excuse to depreciate the rupee, he added.
($1 = 40.22 rupees) -- Karachi newsroom 9221-5685192)
